solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Item of wear that’s never worn out

definitions.text: Item of wear that’s never worn out

blocks.clueFragment: Item of wear that’s never worn out
blocks.note: surface reading: a garment so durable it never wears out
setter's reading: never worn on the outside, because it goes beneath other clothes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Worn out' suggests threadbare clothing; read literally it means worn on the outside, which this item never is.
explanation.definitionFit: Underclothing such as vests and pants sits beneath outer clothing, so nobody wears it on show.

clue.text: Kind of people who follow the herd

definitions.text: Kind of people who follow the herd

blocks.note: surface reading: conformist people who copy everyone else

blocks.clueFragment: Kind of people who follow the herd
blocks.note: setter's reading: wandering herdsmen who literally move with their grazing livestock

explanation.walkthrough: 'Follow the herd' is an idiom for conformity; here it is literal, describing pastoral wanderers moving with their animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Wandering pastoral tribes move from pasture to pasture tracking their cattle, sheep or camels.

clue.text: Girl holds no alternative site for Hamlet

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a girl's name
nor introduces a negative alternative, as in 'neither this nor that'

explanation.surface: A girl is keeping Hamlet from having any other location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' looks like a small village, but it is Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare sets his tragedy at the Danish royal castle of that name, at Helsingør.

clue.text: At end of evening, general merriment

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: final letter of the word
Robert E. Lee, the Confederate general

explanation.surface: When the evening winds up, everyone is jolly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' reads as an adjective meaning widespread, but it is a noun: an army general, the crossword favourite Lee.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe joyful delight and high spirits, making them close synonyms.

clue.text: Telephone a teacher – he’ll crack the whip!

blocks.note: to ring is to phone someone
a schoolmaster is a teacher

explanation.surface: Calling a strict teacher who will impose discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack the whip' sounds like strict discipline, but it is literal: the circus figure with a whip.
explanation.definitionFit: The circus presenter directs horses and performers in the big top, traditionally cracking a long whip.

clue.text: Organised relay in good time

indicators.note: to organise is to put things into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A well-run relay race finishes quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In good time' reads like a race time; it is the definition, meaning ahead of schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Arriving before the appointed hour means arriving with time to spare, ahead of schedule.

clue.text: Swingers’ bar

blocks.note: surface reading: a pub or nightclub frequented by swinging partygoers
setter's reading: acrobats who swing high above a circus ring hold a horizontal bar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swingers' suggests a louche nightspot; the swingers are aerial acrobats and the bar is the one they hang from.
explanation.definitionFit: The circus apparatus is a short horizontal pole hung on two ropes, on which acrobats swing.

clue.text: Faultlessly dressed – like perfect partners?

blocks.note: first meaning: wearing a perfect suit
second meaning: well matched to each other

explanation.surface: A couple turned out immaculately, as flawless as their match.
explanation.walkthrough: The literal sense is wearing a suit perfectly; the idiom describes a couple who are an excellent match.
explanation.definitionFit: Being well matched is the idiomatic sense, while dressing in a flawless suit is the literal one.

clue.text: Old coppers found bike

blocks.note: first meaning: two old British bronze coins, a penny and a farthing (a quarter of a penny)
second meaning: a Victorian bicycle with a huge front wheel and tiny rear one

explanation.surface: Some old policemen came across a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police officers, but it means copper coins; the penny and the farthing were old British ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian cycle took its name from the contrast between a large penny coin and a small farthing.

clue.text: The estate needs me for organisation

indicators.note: organisation means arranging into order, so the letters are put in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A landowner's estate claims it needs someone to run it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needs' looks like the verb joining definition to wordplay, but it is part of the letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A demesne is land attached to a manor and held by its lord, an old term for a landed property.

clue.text: Hastened back with class report

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: hastened means ran
a rate is a grade or class, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: Someone hurried back to school carrying the class report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class report' looks like a school document; 'class' belongs to the wordplay and 'report' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To report events is to give an account or tell the story of them, a synonym.

clue.text: Poet of golden study

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a den is a private study room

explanation.surface: A writer known for his golden study of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golden study' reads as a fine piece of scholarship; it is two parts, a chemical symbol and a room.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was an Anglo-American twentieth-century writer of verse, author of 'Funeral Blues'.

clue.text: Highest peer many found out of place

indicators.note: things out of place are disordered, so the letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Many think the top-ranking lord is out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highest peer' looks like a noun phrase about nobility; 'Highest' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The empyrean was the loftiest heaven in ancient cosmology, so as an adjective it means celestial, uppermost.

clue.text: One politician finished his career bankrupt

indicators.note: to career is to rush about wildly and out of control, so the letters go astray

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a Member of Parliament
finished means over
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician whose career ended in financial ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' is a noun in the surface, but here it is the verb meaning to hurtle wildly. 'Bankrupt' is a verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To bankrupt someone is to ruin them financially and make them poor, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Tearful student Mary chose to have special treatment

indicators.note: treating material specially means working it into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: L for learner, as on a British learner-driver plate
taken as written

explanation.surface: A weepy student called Mary insisted on being treated specially.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tearful student' reads as one description of Mary, but 'Tearful' is the definition and the student gives a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lachrymose comes from Latin lacrima, meaning a tear, and describes someone given to weeping.

clue.text: A knot seamen consider dangerous

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase, standing for the thing sailors fear

blocks.note: first meaning: the square knot sailors use when shortening sail
second meaning: a ridge of rock or coral near the surface that can wreck ships

explanation.surface: Sailors regard a certain knot as risky.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the knot itself is dangerous; really the knot is one meaning and the hazard to shipping is another.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors tie the square knot when shortening sail, and they steer clear of rocky or coral ridges below the waterline.

clue.text: Labour candidate? He’s admitted taking dirty money in return

indicators.note: a return is a journey back the way you came, so the letters run backwards
to admit and to take in both mean letting something inside, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
filthy lucre is money gained dishonestly

explanation.surface: A Labour Party candidate confesses to taking bribes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour candidate' suggests a British Labour Party politician, but the labour is one of the twelve tasks of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek hero was set twelve labours, so he is the figure put forward to perform them.

clue.text: One among the lesser folk in feudal times

definitions.text: One among the lesser folk in feudal times

indicators.note: something among others sits in their midst, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone belonging to the lower orders in medieval society.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer and also points to where it sits, spanning two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval peasant bound to a lord's land was among the lowliest members of feudal society.

clue.text: Traveller allowed key is satisfied

blocks.note: a rep is a travelling sales representative
let means allowed
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: A traveller who was given a key is content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' suggests a door key, but it is a musical key, one of the letters A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: Replete means full up after eating, well fed and so contented, synonymous with sated.

clue.text: O Valentine!

blocks.note: first meaning: the letter O stands for love, the zero score in tennis
second meaning: a romantic card sent on 14 February

explanation.surface: A lovelorn cry addressed to a sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'O' looks like a poetic exclamation; it is the letter that means love, a nil score in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: A Valentine is a romantic note, and O is literally the character that means nil or love in scoring.

clue.text: Terrible strain on a ruler

indicators.note: something terrible is in a dreadful state, so these letters are wrecked and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Governing puts dreadful pressure on a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' could be a measuring stick; here it is a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsarina was a Russian empress, a female sovereign who reigned over the empire.

clue.text: Where to keep the money when you’ve made a profit

blocks.note: first meaning: inside a pouch in your clothes
second meaning: financially ahead

explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase is both a literal place for cash and the idiom for having gained money on a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Coins go literally inside a trouser pouch, and the idiom means ahead financially after a transaction.

clue.text: It’s cold, we hear, in the country

indicators.note: what we hear is what is spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: cold means chilly

explanation.surface: People say it's cold in a certain nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the South American country, with its icy south, is said to be chilly.
explanation.definitionFit: Chile is the long narrow South American nation on the Pacific coast, a sovereign state.

clue.text: Jar in which pound may be kept in ready money

indicators.note: to keep something in is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: ready money is cash
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A jam jar used to store pound coins among spare cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jar' looks like a container for coins, but it is a verb meaning to grate or conflict.
explanation.definitionFit: Colours or opinions that jar are discordant, and to be discordant is to conflict harshly.

clue.text: Start work in French

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
en is the French for in

explanation.surface: Begin a job in the French language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start work' reads as one instruction; 'Start' alone is the definition and 'work' is a catalogue abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To start a meeting or an event is to begin or launch it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Honorary professors – ie retired but retaining integrity

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the letters run backwards
to retain is to keep hold of, so one piece holds another inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
merit is worth or excellence of character

explanation.surface: Honorary professors have stopped working but kept their principles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' fits honorary professors perfectly, which hides its job as the reversal signal. 'Integrity' is a loose match for merit.
explanation.definitionFit: Emeritus, plural emeriti, is the title kept by academics after they leave office, held as an honour.

clue.text: Back seat taken by passengers

blocks.note: surface reading: the rear seats of a car where passengers sit
setter's reading: the rear seat of a motorcycle, behind the rider

explanation.walkthrough: The clue suggests the back of a car; the vehicle is really a motorbike, whose rear perch carries a passenger.
explanation.definitionFit: On a motorcycle the rear saddle behind the rider is where a passenger sits.

clue.text: Large marine mammal in mammoth close-up

blocks.note: a mammoth was a prehistoric elephant
to seal is to close up

explanation.surface: A huge sea creature seen in an enormous close-up photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mammoth' reads as an adjective for huge and 'close-up' as a photograph; they are a noun and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The biggest pinniped, named for the male's trunk-like nose, weighs up to four tonnes.
